extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, and courts (legal practitioners and scholars dealing with re-issue/amendment of patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive standards governing when and how a granted patent may be surrendered and re-issued to correct, perfect, or clarify the specification, drawings, model, or claims without impermissibly adding new matter or changing the invention. Focuses on what original disclosure must show and what alterations re-issue may legitimately make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of surrender and re-issue is not to introduce new features, ingredients, or devices into the patent, but to render effectual the actual invention for which the original patent should have been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue is to correct or perfect a defective or insufficient description (including the Claim) to give effect to the invention the patentee intended to secure; it is not to broaden the patent by adding new features beyond what was described, suggested, or substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of invention judged by comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a re-issued patent is for the same invention as the surrendered original must be determined by a comparison of the specifications and drawings of the two patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question of identity is one of construction (law), not of extrinsic evidence; courts compare the face of the instruments (specifications, drawings, model) to decide whether the inventions are substantially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: No claiming matters inconsistent with original specification/drawings/model
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot claim matters inconsistent with the specification, drawings, and model of the original, even if such matters were claimed in the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in the re-issue that are inconsistent with the original disclosure are invalid; re-issue cannot be used to assert rights to elements not supported by the original patent documents (see Ex parte Warren and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original disclosure may appear in specification, drawings, or model
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor's attempt to describe and claim the invention may appear in the original specification, the drawings, or the Patent Office model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the attempt to cover the alleged subject-matter is shown in any one of these (and can be reasonably interpreted in light of the actual invention), re-issue may be permissible; the model may be used as evidence even if later lost, provided other records are consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No parol (oral) proof to add matter not indicated
rubrics_metrics.description: No parol proof is admissible to show that the inventor intended to describe or claim matter not indicated to some extent in his original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters must appear in the written specification, drawings, or model; oral testimony cannot be used to justify inclusion of new matter in a re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial-indication test for original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The original specification, drawings, or model must afford some substantial indication or suggestion of the actual invention intended to be monopolized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor cannot express the idea with sufficient particularity (words, pictures, materials), the matter may lie outside the industrial domain or requires a new application; re-issue requires that the original at least substantially indicate the claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: If original fails to describe real invention, use new application
rubrics_metrics.description: If the original patent does not describe the real invention, the remedy is a new application and patent, not a re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue cannot be used to introduce wholly new inventions that were not substantially indicated in the original; several cases (James v. Campbell, etc.) emphasize that re-issue is not a substitute for a new patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test: would original have matched re-issue absent substantive defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue is sufficiently indicated in the original whenever the Patent Office or courts, examining the original in light of the actual invention or the perfect re-issue specification, can perceive that if the original claims and descriptions had been free from substantive defects the inventions claimed originally and in the re-issue would have been identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical test used by the Office and courts: re-issue is allowed to correct substantive defects that masked identity, provided the original documents point toward the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office model alone insufficient to support new claim unless inventor's intent shown
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office model alone is not sufficient basis for a new claim in a re-issue unless it also appears that the inventor originally intended to claim the feature in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A model that contradicts the drawings and specification cannot by itself justify an expanded re-issue; model evidence must be corroborated by the written disclosure or other contemporaneous records (see Flower v. Detroit, Ex parte Hunt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot wholly change character of the original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot be granted if it wholly changes the character of the original invention as it appears in the specification and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While re-issue may correct and clarify, it must preserve the essential character of the originally described invention; wholesale substitution of a different invention is forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may include matters necessarily implied by original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may include matters not explicitly described if they were really parts of the original invention and necessarily implied by what was actually described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts allow inclusion of elements that are implicit in the original disclosure (James v. Andrews, Ex parte Siemens), but such inclusion must be reasonably supported by the original description, drawings, or model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language variance allowed if identity of subject-matter preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Variances between the descriptions and claims of the original and the re-issue are permissible so long as the identity of the subject-matter is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in wording, titles, or descriptions do not defeat re-issue provided the same invention is intended; re-issue may use different language to clarify or narrow/expand claims within the original scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-machine patents: specification may be made more certain but not broader
rubrics_metrics.description: In re-issue of patents other than machine patents, the specification may be made more certain or the claim made to correspond with the specification, but not made broader than the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-machine cases, re-issue can clarify or tighten description/claims but cannot add new substantive matter beyond what the original indicated (contrast with machine-patent limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may make definite what was previously only inferable
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may make definite what was before reached only by inference in the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue can cure vagueness or uncertainty by explicitly describing and claiming what the original implied, so long as the implied matter truly belonged to the original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may be enlarged or restricted; description covering more than claims is immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: In a re-issue that enlarges the claims the claims alone are involved, and if the Description covers more than the claims it is of no consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue can restrict or enlarge claims consistent with the original invention; the mere fact that the description mentions more does not control the claim scope if not properly claimed originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper multiplication of claims does not invalidate patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An improper multiplication of claims in the re-issue does not affect the patent; the superfluous claims are void but the valid claims remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive or redundant claims in a re-issue can be disregarded rather than voiding the entire re-issued patent (e.g., Dederick v. Cassell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may restate invention and claim essential but unclearly stated features
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may restate the invention and claim such essential features as are not clearly stated in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original failed to clearly express essential features, re-issue can be used to put them into proper form, provided support exists in the original disclosure (Woven Wire Mattress Co. v. Wire Web Bed Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may claim matters found in original description though not in original claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may claim matters that are found in the original Description even though the inventor made no attempt to insert them in his original Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims originally omitted but supported by the description may be embraced in a re-issue, subject to the usual support/indication limits (Eickemeyer Blocking Mach. Co. v. Pearce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot expand beyond what was substantially described, suggested, or indicated
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue cannot include anything not substantially described, suggested, or indicated in the specifications, drawings, or model of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recurrent limiting principle: re-issue must remain within the sphere of the original disclosure; substantive additions that were not indicated render the re-issue invalid as to those additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission or alteration of words permitted so long as invention not enlarged
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may omit ambiguous words of the original or add new words more accurately descriptive of the invention without enlarging the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing language (including omitting ambiguous terms or correcting spelling/names) is allowed provided the change does not broaden the patented subject-matter (e.g., Allen v. Blunt; Perry examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and drawings in machine patents may be amended only by each other
rubrics_metrics.description: In machine-patents the model and drawings can be amended only by each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections in machine patents are constrained because models/drawings and specification are interdependent; changes must be consistent and cannot use one to override the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction according to state of the art at original filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Original and re-issued patents are construed according to the state of the art at the date of the application for the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of both original and re-issue should be grounded in the art and knowledge existing when the original was filed (Eachus v. Broomall; Gameau v. Dozier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office model cannot alone justify new claim in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office model alone is not a sufficient basis for a new claim in a re-issue unless corroborated and showing original intent to claim the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model evidence must not contradict drawings/specification and must be interpreted with caution; office model alone cannot create entitlement to new matter (reiterating multiple citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter once described as essential cannot be omitted in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter once described in the original specification as essential to the invention cannot be omitted in the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential elements originally presented as required cannot be removed in a re-issue to broaden or materially alter the invention; omission of essential matter is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may include new drawings based on original specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may contain new drawings based on the original specification; the drawings of the re-issue may contain features not shown in the original drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New drawings are allowed if they are within the scope of the original disclosure and serve to clarify or fully set forth the same invention; additional drawing features that extend beyond abandoned matter may be reformed or invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may correct mistakes as to effect produced (not by disclaimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake in the original patent as to the effect produced by the use of the invention may be corrected by re-issue, not by disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue is the vehicle to fix substantive errors about the invention's operation or effect (Schillinger v. Gunther); disclaimer is not the means for such corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may describe the art and advantages more fully
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue may contain a fuller description of the state of the art, the nature of the improvement, and the disadvantages obviated by its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue can expand descriptive background, explain advantages, and show how difficulties may be avoided, provided these additions do not change the invention's scope beyond what the original indicated (Robertson v. Secombe Mfg. Co.).
